# Design

This chapter presents the design of the prototype tool proposed in this dissertation. Throughout this chapter, the term impact is used to refer to the measurable effects of refactorings on quality metrics - specifically ΔSize, ΔCVEs, and ΔWarnings - consistent with the title of this dissertation, Dockerfile Refactorings: Detection and Effects. It describes the planned architecture, its design objectives, and the justification for each decision made. The chapter is grounded in the five rapid experiments conducted prior to this phase, which empirically validated the feasibility of each system component before its inclusion in the design. This approach is consistent with the Design and Development activity of the Design Science Research (DSR) methodology \[11\] adopted in this dissertation.

Table 5.1 summarises the five rapid experiments, mapping each one to its objective, the method used, the observed result, and the system component whose design it grounds. The Dockerfile pairs, measurement scripts, and raw outputs of each experiment are kept in a dedicated /experiments/ folder of the project's public GitHub repository, so that every result reported below can be inspected and reproduced.

The chapter is organised as follows. ## Prototype Tool

### Technical Description

The prototype tool is a Python-based analysis system that receives as input a Git repository path and two commit identifiers, extracts the Dockerfile at each commit from the version history, detects whether a structural refactoring occurred between them, classifies that refactoring according to its primary quality dimension, and produces an impact report quantifying the changes across three quality axes: Performance, Security, and Maintainability.

The selection of Python 3 as the implementation language was determined by the rapid experimentation phase: all five experiments were conducted in Python, and the libraries validated in those experiments - GitPython, dockerfile-parse, and the Docker SDK - are all Python-native. This eliminates any interoperability risk that would arise from selecting a different language and ensures that the prototype can be built directly on top of the validated experimental scripts.

The interaction with the Docker daemon is handled exclusively through the Docker SDK for Python \[Exp. 4\], which communicates directly with the daemon via the Unix socket and returns image sizes as raw byte integers. This is architecturally preferable to parsing the output of the Docker CLI, which rounds values and introduces imprecision. Experiment 4 confirmed that this call returns an exact byte count - 189,410,351 bytes (180.64 MB) for the single test image used in that experiment - a precision level that would be rounded away by the CLI. This precision is essential because the Performance Analyzer computes the size delta by subtracting two such byte counts, and CLI rounding would distort small deltas.

Version history access is handled by GitPython \[Exp. 3\], which navigates the Git object model natively, retrieving the Dockerfile content at any commit as a byte stream without requiring a working tree checkout or filesystem write operations. Experiment 3 validated this approach against the public repository docker/getting-started (commits 2bca273 and 2981665), confirming that two distinct Dockerfile versions can be retrieved correctly with fewer than ten lines of Python code.

Dockerfile parsing is handled by the dockerfile-parse library \[Exp. 5\], which reconstructs multi-line RUN instructions - those split across physical lines using the backslash continuation character - into their logical single-unit representation. This reconstruction is critical for the Detection Engine: without it, a single logical command spread over eight lines would be miscounted as eight instructions, producing false detection results. Experiment 5 confirmed that the library correctly identifies four logical RUN instructions in a Dockerfile where they span multiple physical lines, and one logical instruction in the consolidated version.

Security and Maintainability metrics are collected using Trivy and Hadolint \[10\] respectively, both of which were validated in Experiment 2 with JSON-formatted output. Trivy scans the built Docker image for known CVEs, producing a structured results array with vulnerability identifiers and severity levels. Hadolint performs static analysis on the Dockerfile text, producing a flat array of rule violation objects. Experiment 2 confirmed that both schemas are stable and programmatically parseable, providing the foundation for the Data Extractor component.

### Planned Changes in the System

The current state of Dockerfile maintenance is characterised by the absence of systematic feedback. When a developer applies a refactoring, whether consolidating RUN instructions, updating a base image, or adding cache cleanup, the impact of that change on image size, vulnerability exposure, and structural quality is never actually measured, since decisions are typically based on general knowledge of best practices rather than on empirical evidence. This lack of systematic verification means that improvements are assumed rather than confirmed, leaving the real effects of the applied refactoring unknown.

The prototype tool addresses this gap by introducing a systematic measurement cycle, replacing this opacity with quantifiable evidence of the actual impact produced. For each pair of commits where a refactoring is detected, the system computes three delta values: ΔSize (the change in image size in bytes and as a percentage), ΔCVEs (the change in vulnerability count by severity level), and ΔWarnings (the change in Hadolint rule violations classified by quality dimension). Together, these three values constitute the empirical evidence base for what a refactoring actually achieved.

Four isolated proof-of-concept experiments were conducted prior to this design phase to establish empirical baselines for each delta metric. Each experiment applied a single refactoring to a minimal Dockerfile pair, ensuring that observed deltas are attributable to the refactoring under test and not to confounding changes.

PoC-1 - Inline RUN Instructions (R01): consolidating four separate RUN instructions into a single chained command produced a Delta Size of -187,346 bytes, a Delta Warnings(DL3059) of -3 (complete elimination of the consecutive-RUN smell), and a Delta CVEs of 0. The small size delta reflects a minimal test case; production Dockerfiles with a larger number of instructions are expected to yield proportionally greater reductions.

PoC-2 - Update Base Image TAG (R02): replacing the ubuntu:latest tag with the explicit ubuntu:22.04 tag produced a Delta Warnings(DL3007) of -1, eliminating the latest-tag smell. Because ubuntu:latest is a mutable tag, its resolved version is recorded alongside the experiment artefacts; at measurement time it resolved to Ubuntu 26.04. The size and CVE deltas of this PoC depend on that mutable baseline and are therefore not treated as stable reference values; only the DL3007 elimination is invariant across runs.

PoC-3 - Update Base Image (R10): replacing the ubuntu:22.04 base image with the minimal alpine:3.19 image produced a Delta Size of -26,317,308 bytes and a Delta CVEs of -25, with no Hadolint rule specific to this refactoring. This is the most impactful refactoring in the set, demonstrating that the choice of base image simultaneously affects both the performance and security dimensions, reducing image size and attack surface together.

PoC-4 - Replace ADD with COPY (R08): replacing an ADD instruction that copies a regular file with the equivalent COPY instruction produced a Delta Warnings(DL3020) of -1, with a negligible size delta of +1 byte and a Delta CVEs of 0. The change is purely structural, eliminating the implicit-extraction risk associated with ADD without affecting image size or vulnerability exposure.

These four baselines serve as the acceptance criteria for the verification and validation strategy described in Section 5.1.6, and as reference values for the implementation phase in Chapter 6. The prototype automates the entire measurement process, transforming what required manual invocation of three separate tools into a single programmatic call.

### Challenges

Three engineering challenges shaped the design of the prototype and must be resolved for the system to produce reliable results.

The first challenge is multi-line RUN instruction parsing. Dockerfiles commonly express a single logical shell command across multiple physical lines using the backslash continuation character. A parser that operates at the line level will fragment a single logical RUN instruction into multiple tokens, causing incorrect instruction counts and false refactoring detections. The dockerfile-parse library resolves this by exposing logical instruction objects regardless of their physical line count, as validated in Experiment 5. The Detection Engine is designed to operate exclusively on this normalised representation.

The second challenge is JSON schema heterogeneity. The Data Extractor must aggregate metrics from two tools with incompatible output structures. Hadolint produces a flat array of warning objects with fields code, level, line, and message. Trivy produces a deeply nested structure with a Results array, each element of which contains a Vulnerabilities sub-array. A delta computation that is arithmetically valid requires both schemas to be normalised into a common internal representation before any comparison is performed. Experiment 2 confirmed the structure of both schemas, providing the ground truth for this normalisation design.

The third challenge is consolidation-versus-deletion ambiguity. When the count of RUN instructions decreases between two commits, the change may be either a consolidation refactoring or a simple deletion of an instruction. These are structurally distinct operations with different quality implications. The Detection Engine must distinguish between them through a content preservation check: if the command tokens of the eliminated instructions are recoverable within the surviving instruction, the change is classified as a consolidation; if they have disappeared without trace, the change is classified as a deletion and is not reported as a refactoring.

### Functional and Non-Functional Requirements

The functional requirements are derived directly from the experimental findings and are organised by system component.

RF1 - VCS Connector: The system shall extract the complete textual content of the Dockerfile at two user-specified commits from a local Git repository, using programmatic blob-level access without requiring a working tree checkout. \[Validated in Experiment 3\]. Acceptance criterion: Dockerfile content retrieved at two commits is byte-identical to the content stored in the Git object database

RF2 - Detection Engine: The system shall parse both Dockerfiles into their canonical logical instruction representations and determine whether the structural change between them constitutes a supported refactoring type. For each detection, the engine shall identify the specific instructions involved. \[Validated in Experiment 5\]. Acceptance criterion: the 4-to-1 RUN consolidation from Experiment 5 is correctly identified as Inline RUN Instructions.

RF3 - Classification Engine: The system shall map the detected refactoring type to a primary and secondary quality dimension using the extended catalogue presented in Section 5.2, providing the interpretive context for the delta values. Acceptance criterion: all fourteen supported types are correctly mapped to their primary and secondary dimensions as defined in Table 5.3.

RF4 - Performance Analyzer: The system shall build the Docker image for each Dockerfile state and retrieve the image size in bytes via the Docker SDK, returning a signed delta (ΔSize) expressed in bytes and as a percentage. \[Validated in Experiment 4\]. Acceptance criterion: PoC-3 test - Delta Size correctly computed between Dockerfile A (ubuntu:22.04) and Dockerfile B (alpine:3.19): the image size is reduced from 29.7 MB to 3.4 MB, a difference of 26.3 MB (−88.5%). At byte resolution the Docker SDK reports this as a signed Delta Size of −26,317,308 bytes (29,739,039 → 3,421,731 bytes).

RF5 - Data Extractor: The system shall invoke Hadolint and Trivy against each image state using JSON output mode, normalise their heterogeneous schemas into a common metric representation, and return the warning count delta (ΔWarnings) and CVE count delta (ΔCVEs) by severity tier \[Validated in Experiment 2 and PoC tests PoC-1 and PoC-3\]. Acceptance criterion: PoC-1 test - Delta Warnings(DL3059) = -3 correctly computed; PoC-3 test - Delta CVEs = -25 correctly computed from the Trivy JSON output.

RF6 - Report Generator: The system shall produce a structured output presenting the before and after values for each quality metric, the computed deltas, and a trade-off flag when a refactoring that improves one dimension degrades another. Acceptance criterion: Trade-off flag raised when a refactoring that improves its primary dimension degrades a secondary dimension. None of the four proof-of-concept refactorings produced such a case, so the flag remained inactive across the validation set; the mechanism is verified by construction against the delta-sign comparison logic.

The non-functional requirements are anchored in the quantitative results of the proof-of-concept, making them verifiable rather than aspirational.

RNF1 - Metric Precision: The Performance dimension shall be quantifiable at byte-level resolution sufficient to detect significant size reductions. Acceptance criterion: PoC-3 test - the Docker SDK returns the exact byte size of each image, so the 26.3 MB reduction is preserved at full resolution as −26,317,308 bytes rather than being rounded away by CLI text parsing.

RNF2 - Diagnostic Sensitivity: The Maintainability dimension shall be measurable with sensitivity sufficient to detect the complete elimination of relevant Hadolint rule violations. Acceptance criterion: PoC-1 test - Delta Warnings(DL3059) = -3 correctly detected, representing complete elimination of all consecutive-RUN instruction smell violations between Dockerfile A (3 violations) and Dockerfile B (0 violations).

RNF3 - Extensibility: The Detection Engine rule set and the Classification Engine mapping table shall be extensible to new refactoring types without modification of existing component code, following the Open-Closed Principle \[26\]. The prototype supports fourteen types; the architecture must accommodate additional types in future iterations. Acceptance criterion: a new detection rule can be added by implementing one function and one registry entry without modifying existing rules.

RNF4 - Reliability: All external invocations - Docker SDK, Hadolint, Trivy - shall be wrapped in exception handlers that distinguish recoverable errors from unrecoverable failures and surface informative diagnostic messages. Acceptance criterion: build failure, daemon error, and missing Dockerfile each produce a distinct informative exception.

RNF5 - Reproducibility: The system shall record the analysis timestamp and the Trivy database version in every report, enabling future re-runs to identify whether differences in CVE counts are attributable to Dockerfile changes or to CVE database updates. Acceptance criterion: every generated report contains timestamp and Trivy database version fields.

### Architecture Design

The prototype tool is structured as a sequential data pipeline in which each stage transforms a well-defined input into a well-defined output consumed by the next stage. This architecture was chosen over alternative approaches - such as an event-driven or service-oriented design - because the analysis is inherently sequential at the coarse level: version extraction must precede detection, which must precede classification, which must precede metric collection. The pipeline architecture also ensures deterministic, reproducible execution consistent with RNF5.

Three architectural approaches were considered. An event-driven architecture was rejected because it cannot enforce the strict causal dependency chain required by this analysis: each stage depends on the typed output of the previous stage - version extraction must produce Dockerfile strings before detection can operate, and detection must produce a DetectionResult before classification can proceed. A component that consumes an event before its predecessor has completed would receive incomplete data, producing unreliable results. A service-oriented architecture was rejected because exposing each pipeline stage as an independent network service would introduce inter-service communication overhead and interoperability risks that contradict the Python-native design constraint established during the rapid experimentation phase. The sequential pipeline was selected because MSR-based analysis inherently follows a structured sequence of repository selection, data extraction, and analysis steps \[20\], and this architecture maps directly onto the validated experimental scripts, enforces the causal ordering of operations, and ensures that identical inputs always produce identical outputs.

The pipeline is expressed as the following transformation sequence, which defines the execution order of the components:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 5.1 - Sequential architecture of the prototype analysis pipeline, showing the execution order of the components. The data dependencies between components are detailed in Figure 5.2.

At the metric collection stage - between the Classification Engine and the Report Generator - the three quality dimensions are measured in parallel. The Data Extractor dispatches Hadolint (Maintainability) and Trivy (Security) concurrently while the Performance Analyzer retrieves the image size via the Docker SDK. Since these three operations are mutually independent - none requires the result of another - parallel execution is the natural architectural choice, reducing the total metric collection time from the sum of three sequential operations to approximately the duration of the slowest one. Each branch produces a typed metric object that is aggregated by the Report Generator. Although the metric collection stage executes after classification, the Performance Analyzer and the Data Extractor operate on the Dockerfile pair produced by the VCS Connector, not on the output of the Classification Engine; the classification is consumed only by the Report Generator, where it provides the interpretive context for the measured deltas.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 5.3 - Use case diagram of the Dockerfile refactoring analysis tool.

The tool exposes a single use case to its user, a developer or researcher: analysing the refactoring applied between two commits of a Dockerfile. The user provides the repository and the two commit identifiers, and the analysis then runs to completion without further interaction, producing the impact report in JSON format. The simplicity of this view reflects the design of the tool as a single-purpose, non-interactive analysis pipeline.

Figure 5.4 shows the deployment view of the prototype, identifying where each part of the system executes at runtime.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 5.4 - Deployment diagram of the prototype, showing the Python application, the Docker daemon, and the tool and image containers.

The prototype runs as a Python application on the host machine and delegates all container operations to the Docker daemon, with which it communicates through the Docker SDK over the Unix socket. The Hadolint and Trivy tools execute as containers managed by this daemon, alongside the images built from Dockerfile_A and Dockerfile_B. Hadolint analyses the Dockerfile text, while Trivy scans the two built images. Running the tools as containers keeps their versions pinned and removes the need for host-level installation, which supports the reproducibility of the analysis.

### Verification and Validation Strategy

The verification and validation strategy for the prototype is structured across three levels, consistent with standard software engineering practice.

At the unit level, each pipeline component is tested in isolation using the inputs and expected outputs established during the proof-of-concept experiments. For example, the Detection Engine unit test verifies that the Poc-1 Dockerfile pair - four separate RUN instructions consolidated into one - is correctly classified as Inline RUN Instructions with the four original instructions identified. The Classification Engine unit test verifies that the refactoring types are correctly mapped to their primary and secondary dimensions as defined in Table 5.3, using the four proof-of-concept types as test cases.

At the integration level, the interfaces between components are validated by running the complete pipeline against each of the four proof-of-concept Dockerfile pairs and verifying that the typed data structures - DetectionResult, QualityClassification, MetricSet - are correctly produced and consumed at each boundary as specified in Table 5.2.

At the system level, end-to-end behaviour is validated against the four proof-of-concept scenarios. The expected reference values, measured on 2026-05-29, are: PoC-1 (Inline RUN Instructions) - Delta Size = -187,346 bytes, Delta Warnings(DL3059) = -3, Delta CVEs = 0; PoC-2 (Update Base Image TAG) - Delta Warnings(DL3007) = -1, with size and CVE deltas dependent on the mutable ubuntu:latest baseline and therefore excluded as regression anchors; PoC-3 (Update Base Image) - Delta Size = -26,317,308 bytes, Delta CVEs = -25, with no associated Hadolint rule; PoC-4 (Replace ADD with COPY) - Delta Warnings(DL3020) = -1, Delta Size = +1 byte, Delta CVEs = 0. No refactoring in this set degraded a secondary dimension, so the trade-off flag remained inactive. Divergence from these reference values indicates a regression in the pipeline, except for the PoC-2 size and CVE deltas, which vary with the resolved ubuntu:latest version. These reference values serve as regression anchors for the implementation phase described in Chapter 6.

## Extended Refactoring Catalogue

The extended refactoring catalogue constitutes the first contribution of this dissertation, directly addressing Gap 1 identified in Chapter 4: the absence of a structured catalogue that classifies Dockerfile refactorings according to quality dimensions. Building on the fourteen refactoring types identified by Ksontini et al. \[2\], this catalogue introduces an explicit mapping of each type to a primary and secondary quality dimension, derived from the empirical literature reviewed in Chapter 4. The primary dimension identifies the quality goal most directly served by the refactoring. The secondary dimension captures consequential effects on other quality axes.

Building on the work of Ksontini et al. \[2\], this dissertation introduces an explicit mapping of Dockerfile refactorings to quality dimensions. **Table 5.3** presents this extended catalogue, detailing the primary and secondary quality goals for each refactoring type along with their technical justifications:

| ID  | Refactoring Type         | Primary Dimension | Secondary Dimension |
| --- | ------------------------ | ----------------- | ------------------- |
| R01 | Inline RUN Instructions  | Performance       | Maintainability     |
| R02 | Update Base Image TAG    | Maintainability   | Security            |
| R03 | Add ENV Variable         | Maintainability   | -                   |
| R04 | Add ARG Instruction      | Maintainability   | -                   |
| R05 | Extract Stage            | Performance       | Maintainability     |
| R06 | Inline Stage             | Maintainability   | -                   |
| R07 | Sort Instructions        | Performance       | Maintainability     |
| R08 | Replace ADD with COPY    | Maintainability   | Security            |
| R09 | Extract RUN Instructions | Maintainability   | -                   |
| R10 | Update Base Image        | Security          | Performance         |
| R11 | Move Stage               | Maintainability   | -                   |
| R12 | Remove RUN (mv command)  | Performance       | -                   |
| R13 | Update RUN Instruction   | Maintainability   | -                   |
| R14 | Rename Image             | Maintainability   | -                   |

Table 5.3 - Extended Dockerfile refactoring catalogue classifying fourteen types by primary and secondary quality dimensions.

The remainder of this section develops the technical justification for each classification in Table 5.3. For each refactoring, the primary and secondary dimensions are supported either by empirical evidence from the literature or, where no such evidence exists, by a controlled experiment designed for this dissertation (described in Section 5.2.1 and available in the project repository). Each justification also notes any relevant trade-off across quality dimensions.

**R01 - Inline RUN Instructions**

Consolidating consecutive RUN instructions corresponds to fixing the DL3059 smell. Rosa et al. \[17\] identify it as the smell most frequently fixed by developers in open-source projects, with 168 validated fixes, applied to reduce the image size and the number of layers. Durieux \[24\] confirms empirically that smells associated with RUN instructions and package managers produce an average increase of 4.66% in image size, reaching up to 10% in some cases. As a maintainability trade-off, Rosa et al. \[17\] note that automatic consolidation can be too aggressive, merging instructions that would benefit from staying separate, which may reduce the readability of the Dockerfile. The primary dimension is therefore performance, with maintainability as a secondary, conditional effect.

**R02 - Update Base Image TAG**

Pinning a specific version tag instead of latest corresponds to fixing the DL3007 smell. Rosa et al. \[17\] report that this fix is widely accepted by developers, with a 64% acceptance rate in pull requests, and is applied to guarantee reproducible and predictable builds, since the use of latest causes the base image to change in an uncontrolled way over time. Wu et al. \[8\] frame the absence of version pinning as a smell that affects the reproducibility and maintainability of the Dockerfile. Because the main goal is a stable, predictable build, the primary dimension is maintainability, with security as a secondary effect, as pinning a known version also avoids silently inheriting newer, unverified image content.

**R03 - Add ENV Variable**

Adding an ENV variable consists of extracting values written directly in the Dockerfile, such as paths or version numbers, and centralizing them through the ENV instruction. The Docker Documentation recommends using ENV to set commonly used version numbers, so that a single change to one ENV instruction automatically updates the version of the software in the container, easing maintenance. Ksontini et al. \[27\] include Add ENV among the catalogued refactoring techniques. As a security trade-off, both the Docker Documentation \[7\] and Bui et al. \[28\] warn that placing sensitive data in ENV instructions is a security risk, since those values are transferred to the image during the build and remain visible to any user of the image. The primary dimension is maintainability; security appears only as a negative trade-off, not as a benefit, and is therefore not listed as a secondary dimension.

**R04 - Add ARG Instruction**

Adding an ARG instruction consists of introducing build-time identifiers that are needed only while the image is being built, such as an application or package version passed through docker build --build-arg. The Docker Documentation \[7\] describes that build arguments are commonly used to specify component versions, allowing builds with different versions without manually editing the Dockerfile, and making it easier to maintain by declaring versions at the top of the file and reusing the same value in several places. Ksontini et al. \[27\] include Add ARG among the catalogued techniques. As a security trade-off, the Docker Documentation \[7\] warns that build arguments are not suitable for storing sensitive data, since they are visible through the docker history command and may persist in the image metadata. As with R03, the primary dimension is maintainability and security appears only as a trade-off.

**R05 - Extract Stage**

Extracting a stage implements a multi-stage build, separating the build environment from the runtime environment so that only the essential components are included in the final image. Ksontini et al. \[27\] document that this technique is among the most frequently applied by developers and among those that contribute most to reducing image size, since it discards the build dependencies from the final image while keeping only the components required to run the application; in one analyzed case, this approach reduced the image from 1110 MB to 195 MB. The primary dimension is therefore performance, while the separation between build and runtime phases also improves the structure and maintainability of the Dockerfile, which is captured as the secondary dimension.

**R06 - Inline Stage**

Inlining a stage consists of merging or removing a stage from a multi-stage build when the separation into multiple stages provides no benefit, simplifying the structure of the Dockerfile. Ksontini et al. \[27\] catalogue this refactoring but report that it was not performed in any setting of their study, so no measurement of its impact exists in the literature. Its effect was characterized through a controlled experiment, comparing two functionally equivalent Dockerfiles with the alpine:3.20 base image. The three metrics showed no regression: a negligible variation of 117 bytes in image size, no change in Hadolint warnings (zero in both states), and no change in CVEs (zero in both states). The experiment thus shows that the refactoring introduces no regression in performance, smells, or security. Its classification under maintainability follows from the nature of the operation - removing a redundant FROM and a COPY --from simplifies the structure of the Dockerfile - rather than from an improvement quantified by the automatic metrics, which do not capture this kind of structural simplicity.

**R07 - Sort Instructions**

Sorting instructions consists of reordering the Dockerfile instructions, placing the least frequently modified and most expensive ones before those that change often, in order to optimize layer-cache reuse and reduce rebuild time. Zhu et al. \[29\] demonstrate empirically, in a study of 2,000 GitHub repositories, that reordering instructions improves 92.75% of the Dockerfiles, reducing rebuild time by an average of 26.5%, with 12.82% of the files achieving reductions above 50%, while preserving functional similarity in 86.2% of the cases. As a maintainability trade-off, Zhu et al. \[29\] observe that reordering can separate semantically related groups of instructions, reducing readability, with an efficiency loss of about 5.9% when the semantic grouping is restored. The primary dimension is performance, with maintainability as a secondary, conditional effect.

**R08 - Replace ADD with COPY**

Replacing ADD with COPY corresponds to fixing the DL3020 smell. Rosa et al. \[17\] report that this fix has one of the highest acceptance rates among developers, 71%, indicating the recognition of its value for the clarity and predictability of the Dockerfile. Wu et al. \[8\] identify the use of ADD without needing its automatic file-extraction capability as a common smell, with COPY being the recommended practice. On the security dimension, Bui et al. \[28\] classify the use of ADD as a security smell, since the ADD instruction can download and unpack remote files from URLs without any verification, introducing potential security risks that replacing it with COPY removes. The primary dimension is maintainability, given the gain in clarity and explicitness, with security as a secondary effect arising from the removal of ADD's implicit remote-fetching behavior.

**R09 - Extract RUN Instructions**

Extracting RUN instructions moves a complex sequence of shell commands from inside a RUN instruction into an external script file, executed during the build. Ksontini et al. \[27\] omitted this refactoring from their study because it was present in only two Dockerfiles, so no measurement exists in the literature. Its effect was characterized through a controlled experiment, with the alpine:3.20 base image. The three metrics showed no regression: a negligible variation of 410 bytes in image size (corresponding to the added script file), no Hadolint warnings in either state, and no CVEs. Its classification under maintainability follows from the nature of the operation - moving complex logic out of the Dockerfile improves the readability of the main file - rather than from an improvement quantified by the automatic metrics.

**R10 - Update Base Image**

Updating the base image consists of replacing the base image with a lighter and more secure alternative, for example migrating from a full operating-system image to a minimal one such as Alpine, reducing inherited vulnerabilities and image size. Haque and Babar \[30\] demonstrate empirically that vulnerabilities in the base image propagate to the final image, in one case representing 94.2% of the inherited vulnerabilities; rebuilding the same application with a secure base image (node:alpine instead of node:current-slim) reduced the number of vulnerabilities from 69 to 4 and reduced the application size from 183 MB to 127 MB. The authors further show that replacing debian:jessie with debian:buster reduced the high-exploitability and high-impact vulnerabilities by 88.2%, and that using lightweight base images keeps the application small while minimizing vulnerabilities. The primary dimension is therefore security, with performance as a secondary effect, since the two improvements are obtained together.

**R11 - Move Stage**

Moving a stage consists of extracting an entire stage from a multi-stage build into a separate, standalone Dockerfile that can be built independently and reused. Ksontini et al. \[27\] omitted this refactoring from their study because it was present in only two Dockerfiles, so no measurement exists in the literature. Its effect was characterized through a controlled experiment, with the alpine:3.20 base image. The final runtime image remained practically identical in size (a difference of 1 byte), with no Hadolint warnings in either state and no CVEs. The experiment thus shows that moving the stage into a standalone file introduces no regression in the size or security of the final image. Its classification under maintainability follows from the nature of the operation - separating a stage into an independent, reusable Dockerfile modularizes the build process - rather than from an improvement quantified by the automatic metrics.

**R12 - Remove RUN Instruction (mv command)**

Removing a RUN instruction with an mv command consists of eliminating a RUN whose sole purpose is to execute a move, setting the correct destination path directly in the preceding COPY (or ADD) instruction, which removes the additional layers created by the mv. In the absence of an empirical study isolating this refactoring, its impact was measured through a controlled experiment, with the alpine:3.20 base image. Removing two RUN mv instructions produced a measured reduction in image size of 1332 bytes, while the Hadolint warnings (zero in both states) and the CVEs (zero) remained unchanged. The experiment demonstrates a direct, measured benefit on the performance dimension, with no regression in maintainability or security. The primary dimension is therefore performance, supported by the measured size reduction.

**R13 - Update RUN Instruction**

Updating a RUN instruction consists of reformatting the visual and structural content of a RUN, splitting long or complex commands across multiple lines using the backslash, and ordering the arguments alphanumerically. The Docker Documentation \[7\] recommends splitting long or complex RUN statements across multiple lines separated by backslashes to make the Dockerfile more readable and maintainable, and ordering multi-line arguments alphanumerically to ease maintenance, avoid package duplication, and make code reviews easier to read. This is therefore a refactoring oriented toward maintainability, with no change to the behavior of the image, which is why no secondary dimension is assigned.

**R14 - Rename Image**

Renaming an image consists of assigning explicit names to the stages of a multi-stage build, replacing numeric references with readable identifiers. Ksontini et al. \[27\] document that Rename Image is one of the most frequently applied refactoring techniques by developers, with a frequency above 15%, framing it among the refactorings that improve understandability through renaming, thus contributing to the readability and maintainability of the Dockerfile. As the operation only affects how stages are referenced and named, without changing the build result, its impact is confined to the maintainability dimension and no secondary dimension is assigned.

### Experimental Validation of Catalogue Refactorings

Four refactorings in the catalogue - Inline Stage (R06), Extract RUN Instructions (R09), Move Stage (R11), and Remove RUN (R12) - could not be classified from the empirical literature. The reference study of Ksontini et al. \[27\] reports that Inline Stage was not performed in any setting and omitted both Extract RUN Instructions and Move Stage because each appeared in only two Dockerfiles, while no peer-reviewed study isolates the effect of removing a redundant RUN mv instruction. To classify these four refactorings on a verifiable basis, a controlled experiment was designed for each one, following the same three-metric method used in the proof-of-concept baselines of Section 5.1: image size, Hadolint warnings, and CVEs reported by Trivy. Each experiment compares two functionally equivalent Dockerfiles - one before and one after the refactoring - built from the same pinned base image (alpine:3.20), so that the only difference measured is the refactoring itself. The scripts, Dockerfiles, and raw outputs are available in the project repository.

The three metrics establish the impact profile of each refactoring: they identify any dimension on which a measurable benefit occurs and confirm the absence of regression on the others. A null delta is itself a result, since it shows that the refactoring does not degrade that dimension.

R06 - Inline Stage: merging a redundant build stage into a single stage produced a ΔSize of +117 bytes (≈0%), a ΔWarnings of 0 (no Hadolint warnings in either state), and a ΔCVEs of 0. The negligible size delta is attributable to image metadata, since both Dockerfiles produce the same final filesystem. The experiment confirms that inlining the stage introduces no regression in any of the three dimensions; the maintainability benefit, as discussed above, follows from the structural simplification of the Dockerfile.

R09 - Extract RUN Instructions: moving a sequence of seven inline shell commands into an external script produced a ΔSize of +410 bytes (≈0%), a ΔWarnings of 0 (no warnings in either state), and a ΔCVEs of 0. The small positive size delta corresponds to the added script file. The experiment confirms that extracting the RUN logic introduces no regression; the maintainability benefit follows from moving complex logic out of the Dockerfile.

R11 - Move Stage: extracting an entire stage into a separate, standalone Dockerfile referenced by the main one produced a ΔSize of +1 byte (≈0%) on the final runtime image, a ΔWarnings of 0 (no warnings in either state, counting both the main and the extracted Dockerfile), and a ΔCVEs of 0. The experiment confirms that the final runtime image is unaffected; the maintainability benefit follows from the modularization of the build into an independent, reusable file.

R12 - Remove RUN (mv command): removing two RUN instructions whose sole purpose was to execute mv, and setting the destination path directly in the preceding COPY instructions, produced a ΔSize of −1,332 bytes, a ΔWarnings of 0, and a ΔCVEs of 0. Unlike the previous three, this refactoring shows a measured benefit on the performance dimension: eliminating the two redundant layers reduces the image size, with no regression in smells or vulnerabilities. The magnitude depends on the size of the moved files; for larger files or directories, the saving is expected to be greater, since the moved data would otherwise be duplicated across the temporary and final layers.

These four experiments provide the verifiable basis for the classifications of R06, R09, R11, and R12 in Table 5.3. Three of them (R06, R09, R11) confirm the absence of regression and support a maintainability classification grounded in the nature of the operation, while the fourth (R12) demonstrates a directly measured performance benefit.

### Classification Criteria

The assignment of a primary and a secondary dimension follows two rules. First, a dimension is only assigned when it is supported by evidence, whether measured in the literature or observed in a controlled experiment; a dimension is never assigned to suggest importance where no supporting effect exists. Second, when a refactoring affects more than one dimension, the primary dimension is the quality goal that the refactoring is intended to achieve - the direct purpose of applying it - while the secondary dimension captures an effect that follows as a consequence of that operation, without being its main objective.A further rule governs what the assigned dimensions represent. Both the primary and the secondary dimension denote a positive impact - an improvement that the refactoring brings to that quality axis. A negative effect is never recorded as a dimension; instead, it is described as a trade-off within the textual justification. This distinction matters for refactorings that carry a quality risk rather than a quality gain on a given axis. For example, Add ENV Variable (R03) and Add ARG Instruction (R04) improve maintainability, but the possibility of exposing sensitive data through ENV or ARG is a security risk, not a security improvement; this risk is therefore discussed as a trade-off in the justification and is not listed as a secondary dimension. In the same way, the readability cost of aggressive consolidation in Inline RUN Instructions (R01) or of reordering in Sort Instructions (R07) is reported as a maintainability trade-off in the text, while the dimension columns record only the improvement each refactoring is intended to deliver.To illustrate how the primary-secondary distinction is applied: for Update Base Image (R10), the developer's intent when moving to a lighter, more secure base image is to reduce inherited vulnerabilities, so security is primary, while the smaller image size that comes with a minimal base is a consequence, so performance is secondary. For Inline RUN Instructions (R01), the goal is to reduce image size and layer count, so performance is primary, while the readability impact of merging instructions is the consequence, so maintainability is secondary. In each case, the primary dimension answers the question "why is this refactoring applied?", and the secondary dimension answers "what else does it affect?".

### Maintainability Established by the Nature of the Operation

Three refactorings (R06, R09, R11) are classified under maintainability without a directly measured improvement on that axis. This requires explanation, since the controlled experiments for these refactorings report only the absence of regression across the three metrics - image size, Hadolint warnings, and CVEs - and not a positive value for maintainability. The reason is that maintainability, in the sense of structural simplicity and readability, is not something the three automatic metrics are designed to capture: image size and CVE count measure the resulting image, and Hadolint detects specific smells, none of which corresponds to "the Dockerfile is now simpler to read". For these cases, the maintainability classification rests on the definition of refactoring itself. Following Fowler \[1\], a refactoring is a change to the internal structure of software that makes it easier to understand and cheaper to modify without changing its observable behavior. Each of these three operations matches that definition directly: Inline Stage removes a redundant FROM and a COPY --from, Extract RUN Instructions moves complex shell logic out of the Dockerfile, and Move Stage separates a stage into an independent, reusable file. In every case the internal structure of the Dockerfile becomes simpler or more modular, while the build result is unchanged.This is precisely what the experiments establish, and it is the central value of running them. For each of the three refactorings, the measurements show that every metric remains effectively unchanged between the before and after states: image size varies only by a negligible amount (117 bytes for R06, 410 bytes for R09, 1 byte for R11), the Hadolint warning count stays at zero in both states, and the CVE count stays at zero in both states. In other words, the experiments prove that the structural change leaves the observable properties of the image untouched - exactly as Fowler's definition requires, since a refactoring must not change observable behavior. The role of the experiment is therefore not to prove the maintainability gain, but to provide the evidence that this structural simplification is obtained at no cost: it introduces no size regression, no new smells, and no new vulnerabilities. The maintainability benefit follows from the nature of the operation under Fowler's definition, while the experiment guarantees that the benefit does not come at the expense of performance or security.

### Refactorings with a Single Dimension

Several refactorings in the catalogue have no secondary dimension. Refactorings such as Add ENV Variable (R03), Add ARG Instruction (R04), Update RUN Instruction (R13), and Rename Image (R14) act only on the structure or readability of the Dockerfile, without changing the build result; their impact is therefore confined to maintainability, and assigning a second dimension would not be supported by evidence. The same applies to the refactorings whose impact was characterized experimentally (R06, R09, R11): the measured metrics confirm the absence of regression but do not reveal a measurable effect on a second dimension, so none is assigned.

### Distribution of the Catalogue

The distribution of the catalogue, with maintainability as the most frequent primary dimension, reflects the nature of Dockerfile refactorings rather than a classification bias. Many of the catalogued operations are concerned with the structure, readability, and organization of the Dockerfile - naming stages, formatting instructions, extracting values into variables, or moving logic into separate files - which are inherently maintainability-oriented. Where a refactoring does act primarily on performance or security, the catalogue reflects that: Inline RUN Instructions (R01), Extract Stage (R05), Sort Instructions (R07), and Remove RUN (R12) are classified under performance, while Replace ADD with COPY (R08) and Update Base Image (R10) carry security as a primary or secondary dimension. The classification therefore follows the evidence for each individual refactoring, not a target balance across dimensions.

## VCS Connector

### Technical Description

The VCS Connector is the entry point of the analysis pipeline. Its sole responsibility is to retrieve the complete textual content of the Dockerfile at each of the two specified commits, making it available to the Detection Engine as a UTF-8 string. The component interacts exclusively with the Git object model through GitPython, without modifying the repository state or writing any files to the filesystem.

Given a commit SHA, GitPython resolves it to a git.Commit object, from which the commit's tree is accessed. The tree is navigated to the blob corresponding to the Dockerfile path, and its byte content is read through the data_stream interface and decoded to UTF-8. This sequence of operations is idempotent: repeated calls with the same commit SHA always return identical strings, satisfying RNF5.

Table 5.4 compares the two access strategies considered for the VCS Connector:

**VCS Connector**

| **Approach**             | **Reproducible**                | **Validated**       |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| **Shell git show**       | **❌ Shell escaping artefacts** | **❌**              |
| **GitPython (selected)** | **✅ Programmatic blob access** | **✅ Experiment 3** |

Table 5.4 - Version control system access methods considered for the VCS Connector

GitPython was selected over higher-level mining frameworks because the VCS Connector's task is narrow: retrieving the Dockerfile at two known commits. For this, GitPython's programmatic, blob-level access to file content at any commit - without a working-tree checkout - is sufficient and avoids the overhead of a full mining framework. Spadini et al. \[31\] characterise GitPython as the state-of-the-art Python framework for interacting with Git, and propose PyDriller as a more concise mining alternative; that alternative is unnecessary for this task. This access was validated in Experiment 3 against the docker/getting-started repository, satisfying RF1.

### Planned Changes

In the current state of practice, accessing the Dockerfile at a historical commit requires manual invocation of git show &lt;commit&gt;:Dockerfile, followed by saving the output to a file for further processing. This workflow is error-prone, non-reproducible across shell environments, and unsuitable for automation. The VCS Connector replaces this workflow with a programmatic API call that returns the file content as a Python string directly, eliminating shell escaping artefacts and ensuring byte-identical retrieval.

### Challenges

The principal challenge of this component is the handling of repositories where the Dockerfile is not located at the root of the repository tree, but within a subdirectory. The design accommodates this by accepting the Dockerfile path as a parameter rather than assuming a fixed location. A secondary challenge is the handling of commits where the Dockerfile did not yet exist; the component raises an informative exception in this case, allowing the pipeline to abort cleanly rather than producing an empty string that downstream components would misinterpret.

### Functional and Non-Functional Requirements

The VCS Connector must satisfy RF1 fully: it must extract the Dockerfile content at both commits without requiring a working tree checkout. Non-functionally, it must satisfy RNF5 (reproducibility) by ensuring that the same commit SHA always yields the same output, and RNF4 (reliability) by raising specific exceptions for non-existent commits and non-existent Dockerfile paths.

### Design

The component is implemented as a stateless function that accepts the repository path, SHA_A, SHA_B, and an optional Dockerfile path (defaulting to the repository root). It returns a named tuple containing Dockerfile_A and Dockerfile_B as strings. The stateless design ensures that the component has no side effects and can be tested in isolation with any Git repository.

## Detection Engine

### Technical Description

The Detection Engine is the analytical core of the pipeline. It receives the two Dockerfile strings from the VCS Connector and determines whether the structural change between them constitutes a recognised refactoring type. The engine uses dockerfile-parse to decompose each Dockerfile into an ordered list of logical instruction objects - each containing the instruction type and its normalised argument string - and then applies a set of detection rules, one per supported refactoring type.

The prototype implements automated detection rules for all fourteen refactoring types of the extended catalogue presented in Section 5.2, since the catalogue is adopted in full rather than as a selected subset.

**Table 5.5 compares the two parsing strategies considered for the Detection Engine:**

**Detection Engine**

| **Approach**                    | **Multi-line RUN support** | **Python-native** | **Validated**       |
| ------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------- |
| **Regex line matching**         | **❌**                     | **✅**            | **❌**              |
| **dockerfile-parse (selected)** | **✅**                     | **✅**            | **✅ Experiment 5** |

Table 5.5 - Dockerfile parsing strategies considered for the Detection Engine

Regex-based line matching was rejected because Dockerfile instructions can span multiple physical lines through the backslash continuation character \[7\], preventing a line-level parser from reconstructing them into the canonical logical representations required by RF2. The adoption of structural parsing is consistent with the approach taken by DRMiner \[9\], which employs an Enhanced AST to capture the structural complexities of Dockerfile instructions. dockerfile-parse was selected and its ability to correctly reconstruct multi-line instructions was confirmed in Experiment 5, where four logical RUN instructions spread across multiple physical lines were correctly identified as four units, satisfying RF2.

### Planned Changes

In the current state, the existence of a refactoring in a commit can only be identified through manual inspection of the diff, a process that Ksontini et al. \[9\] note is rarely documented by developers. The Detection Engine replaces manual inspection with automatic structural comparison, producing a typed result that names the refactoring and identifies the specific instructions involved.

### Challenges

Beyond the multi-line parsing challenge resolved by dockerfile-parse (Section 5.1.3), the Detection Engine must resolve the consolidation-versus-deletion ambiguity described in Section 5.1.3. It also faces the challenge of rule priority: when a commit modifies the Dockerfile in a way that matches multiple detection rules simultaneously, the engine must apply a deterministic priority ordering. In the prototype, Security-primary rules take precedence over Performance-primary rules, which take precedence over Maintainability-primary rules, reflecting the relative severity of the quality dimensions in a security-sensitive infrastructure context.

### Functional and Non-Functional Requirements

The Detection Engine must satisfy RF2: parse both Dockerfiles into logical representations and identify the refactoring type and affected instructions. It must satisfy RNF3 (extensibility) by implementing each rule as an independent function registered in a central rule registry, so that new types can be added without modifying existing rules.

### Supported Refactoring Types

Before listing the types the prototype supports, it helps to position each one against the tools reviewed in Section 4.4. Table 5.6 maps the fourteen refactorings to the Hadolint rule they address, where one exists, to the coverage provided by DRMiner, and to the implementation decision made for the prototype. Hadolint and DRMiner operate at different levels, so each column is read on its own terms: Hadolint reports individual smells on a single Dockerfile snapshot, while DRMiner is the only tool that detects refactorings across two revisions. The Hadolint column therefore names the smell a refactoring fixes, where one exists, rather than claiming Hadolint detects the refactoring itself. Docker-Parfum is not included here, since Section 4.4.4 positions it as a validation instrument rather than as a comparison baseline.

Only three refactorings map to a specific Hadolint rule: Inline RUN Instructions (DL3059), Update Base Image TAG (DL3007), and Replace ADD with COPY (DL3020). This is expected, since Hadolint checks best-practice violations on a single snapshot and not the structural changes across instructions that most refactorings involve. DRMiner detects twelve of the fourteen types through its Enhanced AST matching, leaving Remove RUN (mv command) and Update RUN Instruction without automated coverage.

The prototype implements detection rules for all fourteen types because they constitute the extended catalogue - the set of most common Dockerfile refactorings identified in the literature - rather than a selected subset, so no exclusion decision needs to be documented. Implementing all of them ensures that the classification defined in the catalogue can be applied to every refactoring the prototype detects.

| --- | ------------------------ | ---------------------- | --------------------- | ------------------------ |
| R01 | Inline RUN Instructions  | DL3059                 | Yes                   | Yes                      |
| R02 | Update Base Image TAG    | DL3007                 | Yes                   | Yes                      |
| R03 | Add ENV Variable         | -                      | Yes                   | Yes                      |
| R04 | Add ARG Instruction      | -                      | Yes                   | Yes                      |
| R05 | Extract Stage            | -                      | Yes                   | Yes                      |
| R06 | Inline Stage             | -                      | Yes                   | Yes                      |
| R07 | Sort Instructions        | -                      | Yes                   | Yes                      |
| R08 | Replace ADD with COPY    | DL3020                 | Yes                   | Yes                      |
| R09 | Extract RUN Instructions | -                      | Yes                   | Yes                      |
| R10 | Update Base Image        | -                      | Yes                   | Yes                      |
| R11 | Move Stage               | -                      | Yes                   | Yes                      |
| R12 | Remove RUN (mv command)  | -                      | -                     | Yes                      |
